questions.explain: Whenever CALCULATE runs inside row context — whether written explicitly or triggered implicitly by referencing a measure — it converts that row context into filter context.

questions.q: Why does context transition happen automatically when you reference a measure inside a calculated column?
options: Measures ignore row context entirely and use only filter context
It doesn't happen automatically — CALCULATE must always be written explicitly
Every measure is implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE behind the scenes
Calculated columns automatically convert into measures when referenced
questions.explain: Because a measure reference is implicitly CALCULATE-wrapped, referencing one from row context (like inside a calculated column) triggers context transition without any visible CALCULATE in your formula.

questions.q: In the Customer Segment example, what does ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey]) do after context transition occurs?
options: Adds a new relationship to the Sales table
Removes the CustomerKey filter entirely
Removes other filters on the Customer table while keeping the filter that context transition just created on CustomerKey
Converts the calculated column into a measure
questions.explain: ALLEXCEPT clears filters from all columns of the Customer table except CustomerKey — preserving exactly the single-customer filter context transition produced.

questions.q: Why does understanding context transition matter, even for formulas you don't write yourself?
options: It only matters for formulas using time intelligence functions
It's required knowledge before you can create any measure at all
It explains how a calculated column, which only sees row context, can produce results that depend on filtering an entirely different table
It has no practical effect on how formulas behave
questions.explain: Recognizing the pattern — something triggered CALCULATE, converting row context into filter context — demystifies formulas that would otherwise look impossible.
